questions.q: A customer types "three" and your code runs int("three") with no try. What happens?
options: ValueError is raised and, since nothing handles it, the program stops
questions.explain: An unhandled exception prints a traceback and ends the program. On a website, the customer gets an error page.

questions.q: In try: quantity = int(text)  except ValueError: print("please type a number"), when does the except block run?
options: Only if int(text) raised a ValueError
Only if there was no error
questions.explain: If the try block works, except is skipped. If a ValueError happens, the rest of try is skipped and except runs.

questions.q: Why is a bare except: (with no error name) a bad idea?
options: It catches every error, even typos in your own code, and hides them behind a wrong message
questions.explain: In the lab, a typo (pirce_paise) made a NameError, and the bare except printed 'please type a number' for valid input.

questions.q: reserve() finds the customer wants 10 earbuds but only 8 are left. What should it do?
options: raise ValueError("only 8 Wireless Earbuds left"), and let the caller decide what to show
questions.explain: The function says WHAT is wrong by raising; the caller catches it and decides HOW to show it.

questions.q: try / except ValueError / else / finally: which blocks run when there is NO error?
questions.explain: else runs only when try had no error; finally runs every time, error or not.

questions.q: The code does try: int("three") except KeyError: .... What happens?
options: Nothing; errors are ignored inside try
The ValueError isn't caught (KeyError doesn't match), so the program stops
Python converts the ValueError to a KeyError
questions.explain: An except only catches the error type it names. Read the traceback's last line and catch that exact type.

questions.q: (Going deeper) Why write class OutOfStock(Exception) instead of always raising ValueError?
options: Callers can catch exactly this problem (except OutOfStock:) without catching unrelated ValueErrors
Exceptions must be classes you write
questions.explain: Your own exception names make the rule clear and let callers handle it precisely. Django does this, e.g. Product.DoesNotExist.

questions.q: (Going deeper) In Bazaar's future Django API, a view raises an error nobody catches. What does the customer get?
options: An HTTP 500 Internal Server Error, with the traceback in the server's log
The traceback on their screen, always
questions.explain: Expected problems should be handled and turned into clear answers (404, 400). Unexpected ones become 500s, and the log keeps the traceback.
